 1          Plaintiff Iron Tribe Fitness (“Plaintiff” or “Iron Tribe”) respectfully submits this request
 2   pursuant to Rule II.A. of the Court’s General Standing Order for referral to a magistrate judge to
 3   resolve two discrete discovery disputes.
 4          First, Defendant has refused to produce documents in response to Plaintiff’s Rule 34
 5   requests—issued in July 2025—in violation of the Court’s August 2025 order denying Defendant’s
 6   prior motion seeking a stay of discovery. ECF No. 36. Specifically, Defendant has refused to
 7   produce documents by pointing to the fact that the Court granted Defendant’s motion to dismiss
 8   in October 2025, contending that the Court’s comments at the October 3 hearing permitting
 9   Plaintiff leave to amend justifies a blanket refusal to produce “discovery on anything other than
10   [the] underlying contracts” themselves. Defendant is wrong, and its refusal to produce responsive
11   discovery is improper “self-help.” Nazemian v. NVIDIA Corp., 2026 WL 323304, at *1 (N.D.
12   Cal. Feb. 6, 2026). As set forth below, Defendant has not filed a new motion seeking a discovery
13   stay, has no basis to withhold discovery it agreed to produce prior to the Court’s October 3 ruling,
14   and, in any event, its proportionality-based objections are entirely meritless in light of Plaintiff’s
15   filing of the operative Complaint. Facebook should be ordered to engage in discovery.
16          Second, consistent with Defendant’s months-long effort to avoid producing responsive
17   discovery, Facebook has refused to agree to reasonable terms in connection with the parties’
18   negotiated Protective Order and ESI Protocol.            During the parties’ negotiations, Plaintiff
19   repeatedly compromised and adopted Defendant’s proposed changes. However, the parties have
20   reached an impasse concerning certain terms on both documents. To resolve their disputes, and to
21   avoid further delay in Defendant’s production of responsive discovery, Plaintiff will respectfully
22   seek the Court to enter Plaintiff’s proposed Protective Order and ESI Protocol.
23          For these reasons and as further described below, Plaintiff respectfully requests the Court
24   refer the parties’ disputes to a magistrate judge.
25                           Defendant’s Unilateral Partial Stay of Discovery
26          Plaintiff filed this action in April 2025, alleging claims arising out of Facebook’s
27   systematic years-long period of overcharging of advertisers. As alleged in the Complaint, while
28   Facebook promised advertisers it was using a “second-price” auction, which charges a winning

 3   highest bid and their own maximum bid. ¶¶16, 18, 74. Although this switch was due to a 2013
 4   coding change, Facebook concealed this from advertisers upon discovering it and never
 5   reimbursed them for the overcharges. ¶¶21, 24, 26, 96, 154. Plaintiff alleges this gives rise to
 6   claims for breach of contract, breach of the implied covenant of good faith of fair dealing, and
 7   violations of California’s Unfair Competition Law’s (“UCL”) “unfair” prong. ¶¶145-61.1
 8            In July 2025, Plaintiff issued its first set of requests for production seeking documents
 9   concerning, among other things: (1) versions of the Help Center webpages that Plaintiff alleges
10   are part of the contract between Facebook and Plaintiff and the class; (2) documents regarding the
11   coding change that gave rise to Plaintiff’s claims and its impact on revenues; and (3) documents
12   concerning the “slow rollout” of the coding fix that corrected Facebook’s auction process.
13            On July 2, 2025, Facebook sought a stay of discovery during the pendency of the original
14   motion to dismiss it filed two weeks before. ECF No. 29. On August 5, 2025, the Court denied
15   the motion, holding that Defendant had not identified “a particular [or] specific need for a
16   protective order,” and failed to meet both factors that would allow (but not require) the Court to
17   issue such order. See ECF No. 36 at 2-3. The Court explicitly rejected Defendant’s argument that
18   a stay should be granted because Plaintiff did not adequately identify which specific contractual
19   promise was allegedly breached, noting that Plaintiff’s implied covenant claim “is based not on
20   the breach of an express provision in the parties’ contract but the expectation of the parties.” Id.
21   at 2. Defendant did not seek reconsideration or otherwise appeal this order.
22            On September 9 and September 25, 2025, the parties held meet and confers concerning
23   Plaintiff’s document requests, during which Defendant agreed to produce documents in response
24   to a number of those requests. At the same time, on September 15, 2025, Plaintiff provided
25   Defendant with proposed custodians, data sources, and a draft ESI Protocol and Protective Order
26   to facilitate Defendant’s collection and production of responsive ESI discovery.2

20   10655253, at *1 (C.D. Cal. Sept. 16, 2009) (that a complaint is “‘untested’ does not, absent a
21   stay…prevent discovery” into the complaint’s allegations); Norco Windows, Inc. v. Hartford Fin.
22   Servs. Grp., Inc., 2005 WL 1353832, at *10 (D. Idaho June 7, 2005) (“all parties have a duty to
23   engage in discovery unless otherwise relieved by the Court”). Moreover, here, the Court clearly
24   did not stay or otherwise limit discovery through any comments about Plaintiff’s forthcoming

 7          In September 2025, Plaintiff prepared drafts of a Protective Order, ESI Protocol, and Rule
 8   502(d) order to govern the parties’ electronic discovery and the exchange of confidential discovery
 9   material. While the parties were able to resolve most of the disputes, and have agreed to a
10   negotiated Rule 502(d) order, the parties have a small number of remaining disputes concerning
11   the ESI Protocol and Protective Order that Plaintiff requests the Court resolve.
12          For example, with respect to the ESI Protocol, the parties have disputes concerning (i) their
13   document preservation obligations (e.g., Plaintiff objects to Defendant’s request to include a
14   provision relieving parties of the obligation to preserve knowingly responsive materials), (ii) the
15   appropriate application of “email threading,” and (iii) Defendant’s refusal to include a standard
16   “custodian” metadata field. With respect to the Protective Order, the parties have disputes
17   concerning, among other things, (i) Defendant’s insistence on provisions requiring Plaintiff to
18   uncover and report potential “leaks” of purportedly confidential material, and (ii) the conditions
19   for disclosure and treatment of “Source Code,” i.e., the coding language underlying Facebook’s
20   advertising auctions at issue in this case.
21          Plaintiff respectfully submits that a prompt resolution of the parties’ disputes concerning
22   the ESI Protocol and Protective Order are needed to facilitate the parties’ production of discovery.

2           The Court dismissed plaintiff’s original complaint because it failed to identify any con-

3    tractual provision in which Facebook promised advertisers that it would use a second-price auc-

7    do so: its Amended Complaint does not identify any contractual language in which Facebook

8    promised to use a second-price auction. Indeed, plaintiff’s opposition nowhere argues that the

9    Amended Complaint identifies such language. Instead, the opposition attempts to excuse this

10   failure by arguing that it is “irrelevant” that the Amended Complaint did not identify a contrac-

11   tual promise to use a second-price auction. Plaintiff’s acknowledged failure—standing alone—is

12   reason enough to dismiss the complaint again.

13          The opening brief also pointed out that the only official Facebook documents identified

14   in the Amended Complaint that even mention a “second-price” auction actually undermine plain-

15   tiff’s theory, as those documents stated that Facebook “may use a generalized second price auc-

16   tion, a Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) auction, or other auction methodologies that sell several

17   similar-type items.” The opposition brief offers no response to this. The opening brief also ex-

18   plained that the Amended Complaint repeatedly cites an article that described Facebook’s auc-

19   tion process as a “black box,” belying plaintiff’s insistence that advertisers “widely understood”

20   Facebook to use a second-price auction. The opposition’s only response is a footnote claiming

21   that by citing this language, which is quoted repeatedly in plaintiff’s own complaint, Facebook

22   somehow “ignores the article.” Plaintiff’s obvious inability to respond to these points under-

23   scores its failure to cure the deficiency identified by the Court when it dismissed the original

24   complaint.

26   guage that says nothing about a second-price auction—i.e., phrases referring to the “minimum

9            Notwithstanding what the opposition asserts, California courts do not “always” consider

10    extrinsic evidence if there is a dispute about what a contract says. Id. at 8. Extrinsic evidence

11    may not be used to “add to, detract from, or vary the terms of a written contract.” Br. at 10

12    (quoting Zenger-Miller, Inc. v. Training Team, GmbH, 757 F. Supp. 1062, 1067 (N.D. Cal.

13    1991)). Instead, extrinsic evidence is admissible only if it “is relevant to prove a meaning to

14    which the language of the instrument is reasonably susceptible.” Pac. Gas & Elec. Co. v. G.W.

15    Thomas Drayage & Rigging Co., 69 Cal. 2d 33, 37 (1968). By contrast, if a contract is “clear

16    and explicit, the parties’ intent is determined solely by reference to the language of the agree-

17    ment.” Marzec v. Cal. Pub. Employees Retirement Sys., 236 Cal. App. 4th 889, 909–10 (2015).

18    In trying to distinguish Facebook’s authority on this point, the opposition brief tellingly omits the

19    phrase “add to” from its discussion of Zenger-Miller. Opp. at 8. But that is precisely what

20    plaintiff is seeking to do—i.e., “add to” the agreement between the parties an obligation to use a

21    second-price auction that appears nowhere in the agreement. Because that is impermissible un-

22    der California law, plaintiff’s extrinsic evidence is irrelevant.

6     plaintiff offers nothing in support of its UCL claim but allegations that are duplicative of its breach

7     of contract claim. It alleges that Facebook acted “unfair[ly]” insofar as it “[u]sed a blended price

8     auction” rather than the “second price auction” it supposedly “represent[ed] publicly” that it used

9     and “[o]vercharged all advertisers due to its use of a blended price auction.” Am. Compl. ¶ 131.

11    ing Facebook “breached its contract” by “charg[ing] advertisers pursuant to a blended price auc-

12    tion” rather than a “second price auction,” thus “overcharg[ing] every advertiser”).

14    to engage in the same alleged conduct that forms the basis of plaintiff’s breach of contract claim.

15    The UCL claim should be dismissed for that reason alone. See Rosell, 2014 WL 4063050, at *6

16    (dismissing UCL claim where plaintiffs failed to “allege a plus factor showing an independent

17    violation of the UCL” or “come up with anything more than breach of contract”).7

19    courts. Taleshpour v. Apple Inc., 549 F. Supp. 3d 1033, 1045 (N.D. Cal. 2021), aff’d, 2022 WL

20    1577802 (9th Cir. May 19, 2022). To state a claim for unfairness under the UCL, a plaintiff must

21    show either (1) that the conduct is “tethered to specific constitutional, statutory, or regulatory pro-

22    visions” (the “tethering test”); or (2) that the harm to the consumer outweighs the utility of the

23    defendant’s conduct (the “balancing test”). See id. The Amended Complaint does neither.

9     I.     This Action Is Time-Barred
10           As shown in Facebook’s opening brief, all of plaintiff’s claims are time-barred. Plaintiff
11    does not dispute that all of its claims are subject to a four-year statute of limitations, as Facebook
12    demonstrated. See Mot. at 6. Nor does plaintiff contest the fact that the complaint is devoid of
13    any factual allegations of purported misconduct later than 2017. See id. at 7. Thus, because the
14    expiration of the applicable statute of limitations “is apparent from the face” of the complaint—as
15    plaintiff does not dispute—“it must be dismissed.” Barnett v. Kapla, 2020 WL 7428321, at *20
16    (N.D. Cal. Dec. 18, 2020) (citing Jablon v. Dean Witter & Co., 614 F.2d 677, 682 (9th Cir. 1980)).
17           Plaintiff’s only argument is that its claims should be tolled under California’s discovery
18    rule, notwithstanding that the statute of limitations lapsed years ago. See Opp. at 9–11. But plain-
19    tiff misapprehends that rule. It does not permit a plaintiff to file suit whenever it likes—even years
20    after the limitations period—and avoid a finding that its claims are time-barred merely by asserting
21    that it did not have “reason to know” of its claims. Id. at 10. Rather, to invoke the rule, a plaintiff
22    “must specifically plead facts to show (1) the time and manner of discovery and (2) the inability
23    to have made earlier discovery despite reasonable diligence.” Fox v. Ethicon Endo-Surgery, Inc.,
24    35 Cal. 4th 797, 808 (2005). “In assessing the sufficiency of the allegations of delayed discovery,
25    the court places the burden on the plaintiff to ‘show diligence’; ‘conclusory allegations will not
26    withstand [a motion to dismiss].’” Id.; see Plumlee v. Pfizer, Inc., 664 F. App’x 651, 653 (9th Cir.
27    2016) (affirming dismissal of complaint because plaintiff “failed to allege any facts that she was
28    unable to discover the factual bases of her claims earlier despite exercising reasonable diligence”).
